::: {.notes}
**Time.** The opening runs 3 minutes. This slide takes 1.

**Facts on the slide.**

- **CITF Databank.** It holds data from studies supported by the Canadian COVID-19 Immunity Task Force. You work on it as a postdoc at McGill under David Buckeridge. Individual-level data are restricted and go to approved requests only.
- **PhD.** University of Toronto, Faculty of Information. Your supervisor was Costis Dallas, whose 2016 paper section 5 covers.
- **Stelida Naxos Archaeological Project.** You have managed its database since 2016.
- **Community infrastructure.** You maintain open-archaeo with Joe Roe, archaeo.social and the Digital Archaeology Maintainathon. You are a Carpentries-certified teacher and a contributor to O-Date.

**To add.** One or two sentences, in your words, on where you stand on open science. The slide gives the facts and leaves your position to you.
:::

## The argument {.s1}

::: {.lines}
Open science rests on a picture of how science works

::: {.fragment}
The picture says little about who does the work and who it serves
:::

::: {.fragment}
Digital curation is where those questions have to be answered
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1.5 minutes.

**Run it.** Press the arrow key once per line.

**The picture.** Section 2 draws it. A scientist asks a question, forms a hypothesis, runs an experiment, collects data and writes a paper. Most of us learned this version in school. Open science adds sharing to the end of it.

**What it assumes.** The picture carries assumptions about data, access, infrastructure, method and labour. Sections 3, 4 and 5 test them, one at a time. The closing table in section 5 lists all six.

**The questions.** Who does the work and who the work serves come up in every section. The cost of the work follows from the first question, and section 5 is built around it.
:::
